transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Hi, thanks. Yeah, um... I guess what finally made me ask for help is that I just keep forgetting little things I normally handle fine. Like, I'm a secretary, so keeping track of stuff is literally my job, but lately I keep forgetting to return calls. Or I'll completely forget to turn in a registration form. 

Actually, that happened with my niece's dance class last week—my sister asked me to drop the form off because her studio is right by my office. They have this really cute recital every spring, they wear these little sparkly tutus, it's just adorable. My sister always makes a big deal out of it and buys like a dozen roses, which I honestly think is a bit much for seven-year-olds, but you know how moms get. She gets so stressed out about the parking there, too, because the lot is tiny. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yeah. I'm just forgetting stuff. Like I'll tell myself to stop for an errand on the way home, like grabbing milk or something, and then I just pull into my driveway and realize I drove right past the store and completely forgot.
Has this kind of forgetfulness and getting sidetracked been something you've dealt with since childhood, or is this a new change for you recently?

Oh, no, it's definitely not new. Even back in elementary school, I was totally that kid. I was always forgetting permission slips, or my homework would just get completely swallowed up in my backpack. I actually had this really bright pink Lisa Frank backpack in third grade—it had the golden retrievers on it, which was my absolute favorite because we had a golden retriever named Buster at home. He was such a good dog, he used to sleep right under the kitchen table while we ate. My dad would always sneak him pieces of toast, even though my mom hated it because she said it made him beg and shed all over the good dining room rug. She was so particular about that rug. 

But anyway, yeah, my mom or my teachers basically had to walk me through everything step by step just to get me to finish any of my school projects. If I didn't have them constantly reminding me what to do next, nothing would ever get done. So, um... yeah, it's pretty much always been a thing.

latest_inference.note: Childhood-onset inattentiveness, forgetfulness, and need for external structure strongly support ADHD (F90.0). Lifelong pattern rules out acquired cognitive disorder (F06.7) and mood/anxiety-related concentration issues (F32.9, F41.1, R41.3), as these typically have later onset or episodic course.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of inattentive symptoms—forgetfulness, losing track of tasks, being easily distracted mid-conversation, needing external structure/reminders to complete tasks—that persist into adulthood and cause functional impairment at work (missed calls, forgotten paperwork) and daily life (missed errands). No evidence of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms is reported, and symptoms are not better explained by an anxiety or mood disorder, supporting a diagnosis of ADHD, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation.
